```{python}
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ── Consistent chart theme ────────────────────────────────
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor":"#F1F5F9","axes.facecolor":"#F1F5F9",
    "axes.spines.top":False,"axes.spines.right":False,
    "axes.edgecolor":"#CBD5E1","axes.labelcolor":"#334155",
    "axes.labelsize":12,"xtick.labelsize":10,"ytick.labelsize":10,
    "xtick.color":"#94A3B8","ytick.color":"#94A3B8",
    "lines.linewidth":2.2,"font.family":"DejaVu Sans",
    "grid.color":"#E2E8F0","grid.linewidth":0.7,
    "legend.fontsize":10,"legend.framealpha":0.92,
    "legend.edgecolor":"#E2E8F0","figure.dpi":130,
})

TEAL="#0D9488"; ORANGE="#F97316"; GREEN="#22C55E"
NAVY="#1A3A5C"; RED="#EF4444"; GRAY="#94A3B8"

# ── Build dataset (same as original) ─────────────────────
np.random.seed(42)
dates = pd.date_range(start="2018-01-01", end="2022-12-31", freq="B")
returns = []
for d in dates:
    if   d < pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01"):  returns.append(np.random.normal( 0.0004, 0.008))
    elif d <= pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"): returns.append(np.random.normal(-0.0008, 0.035))
    else:                                  returns.append(np.random.normal( 0.0005, 0.014))

df = pd.DataFrame({"Date": dates, "Return": returns})
df["Price"]   = 100 * (1 + df["Return"]).cumprod()
df["Trend"]   = df["Price"].rolling(90, center=True).mean()
df["RolVol"]  = df["Return"].rolling(30).std()
df["Period"]  = np.where(df["Date"] < "2020-03-01", "Pre-COVID",
                np.where(df["Date"] <= "2020-06-30", "COVID Shock", "Post-Shock"))

SHOCK = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-01")
mean_r = df["Return"].mean()
std_r  = df["Return"].std()
df["Anomaly"] = abs(df["Return"] - mean_r) > 3 * std_r
anomalies = df[df["Anomaly"]]
```

     SLIDE 1 — WHAT IS A TIME SERIES?
     ═══════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## What Is a Time Series?

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

A **time series** is a sequence of values recorded at regular points in time — daily, monthly, hourly, or any consistent interval.

What makes it different from a normal data table: **the order of rows matters.** Monday is connected to Tuesday. You cannot shuffle the data without losing information.

**Every time series has two parts:**

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:10px;margin-top:12px;">
<div class="card card-teal" style="padding:12px;">
  <div style="font-size:1.3em;margin-bottom:4px;">📅</div>
  <strong>Timestamp</strong><br>
  <span style="font-size:0.85em;color:var(--dgray);">When was it recorded?</span>
</div>
<div class="card card-orange" style="padding:12px;">
  <div style="font-size:1.3em;margin-bottom:4px;">📏</div>
  <strong>Value</strong><br>
  <span style="font-size:0.85em;color:var(--dgray);">What was measured?</span>
</div>
</div>

::: {.info}
💡 **Our example:** Stock market daily returns, 2018–2022. COVID-19 creates a visible "before, during, and after" — perfect for seeing every time series concept clearly.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.5))

ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.12)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Price"], color=TEAL, linewidth=2.0, label="Market Index")
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--", label="COVID Shock begins")

ax.annotate("Calm period\nSmall, regular changes",
            xy=(pd.Timestamp("2019-01-01"), 116),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2018-03-01"), 130),
            fontsize=9.5, color=TEAL, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=TEAL, lw=1.3))
ax.annotate("Sudden shock!\nHuge drop in weeks",
            xy=(pd.Timestamp("2020-04-15"), 88),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2020-06-01"), 74),
            fontsize=9.5, color=ORANGE, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=ORANGE, lw=1.3))
ax.annotate("Recovery\nMore turbulent than before",
            xy=(pd.Timestamp("2021-07-01"), 150),
            xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2021-09-01"), 128),
            fontsize=9.5, color=GREEN, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GREEN, lw=1.3))

ax.set_xlabel("Date"); ax.set_ylabel("Index Value (starts at 100)")
ax.set_title("Stock Market Index — a classic time series", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

     SLIDE 2 — TREND & STATIONARITY
     ═══════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Concept 1 — Trend & Stationarity

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

### 📈 Trend — the Long-Run Direction

The **trend** is the overall direction of the series after smoothing out noise. We find it using a **rolling mean** — averaging the last N observations as we slide along.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.0))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Price"], color=TEAL, linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.28, label="Daily (noisy)")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Trend"], color=NAVY, linewidth=2.6, label="90-day rolling mean (trend)")
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--")
ax.set_ylabel("Value"); ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
The navy line removes the noise — now the **up → crash → recover** direction is obvious.
:::

:::

::: {}

### 🔄 Stationarity — Does It Stay Consistent?

A series is **stationary** when its mean and spread stay roughly stable over time. Almost every time series model requires this.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.8, 3.2), sharex=True)

axes[0].plot(df["Date"], df["Price"], color=RED, linewidth=1.5)
axes[0].set_title("❌ Price level drifts — NOT stationary", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Price"); axes[0].grid(axis="y")

axes[1].plot(df["Date"], df["Return"]*100, color=TEAL, linewidth=0.85, alpha=0.85)
axes[1].axhline(0, color=NAVY, linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--", label="Mean ≈ 0")
axes[1].set_title("✅ Daily % change bounces near zero — stationary", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=TEAL)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Change (%)"); axes[1].set_xlabel("Date")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9); axes[1].grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.darkbar}
**The fix:** Use the **daily % change** instead of the raw level. Changes stay near zero — stationary. The rising price series is not.
:::
:::
:::

---

<!-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE 3 — ROLLING WINDOWS & VOLATILITY
     ═══════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Concept 2 — Rolling Windows & Volatility

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

### 🪟 What Is a Rolling Window?

A rolling window slides along the series and recomputes a statistic using only the **most recent N observations.** This turns a single summary number into a **story over time.**

<div class="step"><div class="step-n">1</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Pick a window size</h4><p>e.g. 30 days — how far back do you look?</p></div></div>
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">2</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Compute the statistic</h4><p>Mean, std dev, sum — whatever you need</p></div></div>
<div class="step"><div class="step-n">3</div><div class="step-b"><h4>Slide forward one day, repeat</h4><p>You now have a value for every date</p></div></div>

### 📊 Volatility = Rolling Std Dev

**Volatility** measures how much the series jumps around day to day. We compute it as the **rolling standard deviation** of daily changes over the last 30 days.

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.8, 4.5), sharex=True)

# Top: returns with rolling mean band
roll_mean = df["Return"].rolling(30).mean() * 100
roll_std  = df["Return"].rolling(30).std()  * 100
axes[0].plot(df["Date"], df["Return"]*100, color=TEAL, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.45, label="Daily change")
axes[0].plot(df["Date"], roll_mean, color=NAVY, linewidth=1.8, label="30-day mean")
axes[0].fill_between(df["Date"],
                     roll_mean - roll_std, roll_mean + roll_std,
                     alpha=0.18, color=NAVY, label="±1 std dev band")
axes[0].axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.6, linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_title("Rolling Mean ± Rolling Std Dev", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Change (%)"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8); axes[0].grid(axis="y")

# Bottom: rolling volatility alone
axes[1].axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
axes[1].plot(df["Date"], df["RolVol"]*100, color=RED, linewidth=2.2, label="30-day volatility")
axes[1].fill_between(df["Date"], df["RolVol"]*100, alpha=0.12, color=RED)
axes[1].axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.6, linestyle="--")
pv  = (df["RolVol"]*100).max()
pdt = df.loc[(df["RolVol"]*100).idxmax(), "Date"]
axes[1].annotate(f"Peak ≈ {pv:.1f}% (4× normal)",
                 xy=(pdt, pv), xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01"), pv*0.82),
                 fontsize=9, color=RED, fontweight="bold",
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=RED, lw=1.3))
axes[1].set_title("Rolling Volatility — when did the series become wild?", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Volatility (%)"); axes[1].set_xlabel("Date")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8); axes[1].grid(axis="y")

fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
⚡ The rolling window turns one number into a timeline — you can see **exactly when** the series became risky, not just that it was risky overall.
:::
:::
:::

<!-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE 4 — STRUCTURAL BREAK & AUTOCORRELATION
     ═══════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Concept 3 — Structural Break & Autocorrelation

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

### 💥 Structural Break — When the Pattern Changes Permanently

A structural break is a point where the series **permanently shifts** its behaviour. Models trained before the break will give wrong answers after it.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.1))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.12)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["RolVol"]*100, color=RED, linewidth=2.0)
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--", label="Break point")

pre_m  = df[df["Date"] < SHOCK]["RolVol"].mean() * 100
post_m = df[df["Date"] > pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30")]["RolVol"].mean() * 100
ax.axhline(pre_m,  xmax=0.47, color=TEAL,  linewidth=2.4, linestyle="-", label=f"Before avg: {pre_m:.2f}%")
ax.axhline(post_m, xmin=0.53, color=GREEN, linewidth=2.4, linestyle="-", label=f"After avg:  {post_m:.2f}%")
ax.set_ylabel("30-day Volatility (%)"); ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.set_title("Volatility before vs after COVID — permanently different", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.darkbar}
Volatility nearly **doubled and stayed there.** Any model built on pre-COVID data now underestimates risk.
:::

:::

::: {}

### 🔁 Autocorrelation — Does the Past Predict the Future?

**Autocorrelation** measures whether today's value is related to yesterday's. If yes, the series has **memory** — useful for forecasting.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.8, 3.4))

periods_ac = [
    ("Before\nCOVID",  df[df["Date"] < SHOCK]["Return"]),
    ("During\nCOVID",  df[(df["Date"] >= SHOCK) & (df["Date"] <= "2020-06-30")]["Return"]),
    ("After\nCOVID",   df[df["Date"] > "2020-06-30"]["Return"])
]

for ax, (label, series), col in zip(axes, periods_ac, [TEAL, ORANGE, GREEN]):
    lags = range(1, min(16, len(series)//3))
    acf_vals = [series.autocorr(lag=k) for k in lags]
    ax.bar(list(lags), acf_vals, color=col, edgecolor="white", width=0.65, alpha=0.85)
    ax.axhline(0, color="#334155", linewidth=1.0)
    conf = 1.96 / len(series)**0.5
    ax.axhline( conf, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.0, linestyle="--", alpha=0.7)
    ax.axhline(-conf, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.0, linestyle="--", alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=col)
    ax.set_xlabel("Lag (days)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Correlation" if ax==axes[0] else "")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 0.5); ax.grid(axis="y")

fig.suptitle("Autocorrelation of Daily Returns\n(bars past dashed lines = significant memory)",
             fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY, y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.info}
During the shock, **lag-1 is significant** — one bad day predicted the next. Panic has momentum. Before and after: far less memory, more random.
:::
:::
:::

     SLIDE 5 — ANOMALY DETECTION
     ═══════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Concept 4 — Anomaly Detection

An **anomaly** is a data point so far from normal that it signals something genuinely unusual happened. We use the **3-sigma rule** — the simplest detector that needs no labels, just the data's own mean and spread.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

<div class="card card-teal" style="margin-bottom:12px;">
<h3>The 3-Sigma Rule</h3>
Flag a point if its distance from the mean is more than 3 standard deviations.
<div class="formula" style="font-size:0.9em; margin-top:10px;">
Flag if: |value − mean| &gt; 3 × std dev
</div>
In normally distributed data, only **0.3%** of points fall that far out — so anything flagged is genuinely rare.
</div>

```{python}
counts = [len(anomalies[anomalies["Period"]==p])
          for p in ["Pre-COVID","COVID Shock","Post-Shock"]]
total  = [len(df[df["Period"]==p])
          for p in ["Pre-COVID","COVID Shock","Post-Shock"]]
pct    = [c/t*100 for c,t in zip(counts,total)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.0))
bars = ax.bar(["Before\nCOVID","COVID\nShock","After\nCOVID"],
              pct, color=[TEAL,RED,GREEN], edgecolor="white", width=0.5)
ax.axhline(0.3, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.4, linestyle="--", label="Expected: 0.3% normally")
for bar, v, c in zip(bars, pct, counts):
    ax.text(bar.get_x()+bar.get_width()/2, v+0.12,
            f"{v:.1f}%\n({c} days)", ha="center",
            fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=bar.get_facecolor())
ax.set_title("% of Days Flagged as Anomaly", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.set_ylabel("% of days"); ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.6))
ax.axvspan(SHOCK, pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30"), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10, label="COVID Window")
ax.plot(df[~df["Anomaly"]]["Date"], df[~df["Anomaly"]]["Return"]*100,
        color=TEAL, linewidth=0.85, alpha=0.55, label="Normal day")
ax.scatter(anomalies["Date"], anomalies["Return"]*100,
           color=RED, s=50, zorder=5, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.6,
           label=f"Anomaly flagged (n={len(anomalies)})")
ax.axhline((mean_r+3*std_r)*100, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.1, linestyle=":", alpha=0.8, label="±3σ boundary")
ax.axhline((mean_r-3*std_r)*100, color=GRAY, linewidth=1.1, linestyle=":", alpha=0.8)
ax.axhline(0, color="#CBD5E1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.axvline(SHOCK, color=ORANGE, linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Date"); ax.set_ylabel("Daily Change (%)")
ax.set_title("Where Anomalies Appear — red dots = flagged days",
             fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis="y")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
⚡ **~9% of COVID-period days were anomalies** — 30× the normal rate of 0.3%. The rule found the crisis automatically using nothing but the data's own statistics.
:::
:::
:::

<!-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE 6 — KEY TAKEAWAYS
     ═══════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Key Takeaways

::: {.two-col}

<div class="tcard">
<div class="tcard-hdr" style="background:#1A3A5C;">
  <span class="tcard-num">01</span>
  <span class="tcard-ttl">Time Series = Ordered Data</span>
</div>
<div class="tcard-bdy">
A time series is values recorded over time where <strong>order matters.</strong> Monday connects to Tuesday. Shuffle the rows and you destroy the information.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tcard">
<div class="tcard-hdr" style="background:#0D9488;">
  <span class="tcard-num">02</span>
  <span class="tcard-ttl">Use Changes, Not Levels</span>
</div>
<div class="tcard-bdy">
Raw values that drift upward forever are <strong>not stationary.</strong> Use % changes instead — they bounce around zero and work with most analysis tools.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tcard">
<div class="tcard-hdr" style="background:#1A3A5C;">
  <span class="tcard-num">03</span>
  <span class="tcard-ttl">Rolling Windows Show When</span>
</div>
<div class="tcard-bdy">
A rolling mean or rolling std dev turns one summary number into a <strong>timeline.</strong> You see exactly when the series changed — not just that it changed overall.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tcard">
<div class="tcard-hdr" style="background:#0D9488;">
  <span class="tcard-num">04</span>
  <span class="tcard-ttl">Structural Breaks Need New Models</span>
</div>
<div class="tcard-bdy">
When behaviour <strong>permanently changes,</strong> old models stop working. Detecting the break point is step one — then you retrain on the new regime.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tcard">
<div class="tcard-hdr" style="background:#1A3A5C;">
  <span class="tcard-num">05</span>
  <span class="tcard-ttl">Autocorrelation = Memory</span>
</div>
<div class="tcard-bdy">
If today's value is linked to yesterday's, the series has <strong>memory.</strong> During COVID, panic had momentum — one bad day predicted the next.
</div>
</div>

<div class="tcard">
<div class="tcard-hdr" style="background:#0D9488;">
  <span class="tcard-num">06</span>
  <span class="tcard-ttl">Simple Rules Detect Anomalies</span>
</div>
<div class="tcard-bdy">
The 3-sigma rule flagged <strong>30× more anomalies</strong> during COVID using only mean and std dev — no labels, no complex model needed.
</div>
</div>

:::

<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0D1B2A,#1A3A5C);border:1px solid #0D9488;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 20px;margin-top:14px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:16px;">
  <span style="font-size:1.6em;">💡</span>
  <p style="color:#CBD5E1;margin:0;font-size:0.92em;line-height:1.6;">These tools work on <strong style="color:#14B8A6;">any data over time</strong> — temperature, hospital admissions, website traffic, energy usage. COVID and the stock market are just our learning example.</p>
</div>
